America needs a conservative party. Here, I mean conservative in the sense of Oakeshott, Burke, or of Rerum Novarum. This is a conservatism that warns when we are outspending our means. This is a conservatism that understands that society is an organic structure that grows and progresses in ways that do not always match the desires of social planners. This is a conservatism that believes that those holding the highest offices should conduct themselves with honor and virtue.  

Ironically, the best model for a future conservatism is precisely the one Vance has opposed most strenuously: the social teachings of Pope Francis and Pope Leo. Laudato Si and Leo's encyclical on AI offer a conservative (in the classical sense) vision: one that actually conserves the ecological sphere in which we live, and the economy through which we interact. 

For instance, read what Francis said of the idea that the Bible gives man dominion over the earth:

"This is not a correct interpretation of the Bible as understood by the Church... The biblical texts are to be read in their context, with an appropriate hermeneutic, recognizing that they tell us to “till and keep” the garden of the world (cf. Gen 2:15). “Tilling” refers to cultivating, ploughing or working, while “keeping” means caring, protecting, overseeing and preserving. This implies a relationship of mutual responsibility between human beings and nature."

At first glance I’m happy about this however the difficulty with political economy and society is that controlled experiments rarely can be performed.  As opposed to say microbiology where doing controlled experiments is routine.  What ends up happening is the possibility that we become the experiment. I’ll remind everyone that Angela Merkel had a PhD in quantum chemistry and things didn’t turn out well for Germany wrt the rise of the far right in response to her little immigration experiment.

But academically trained scientists are permeating a lot of non-scientific fields these days because we deliberately overproduce the labor supply as a result of the structures of the system (or cynically, in an effort to keep labor prices low).

Counterintuitively, it’s actually a tragedy of the commons for the academy: there are way too many academic  scientists competing for too few resources and the diminishing returns on investment are glaringly obvious.  Science done now is purely risk averse, fast, and minimal.  Which means it is a cheap scientific product produced in a pseudo-market with no immediate feedback on its quality. "Friday Night Lights" may be a point of criticism for people who think we put too much importance on athletics, but as a product of a small Texas town, you need to appreciate just what an important cultural institution the public schools are to our rural farm communities. If the computer is so powerful that it can play out every possible move, it ceases to be a challenge.

Tbis points to something I tried to tell Oracle this morning. If you have a computer that is dedicated to database processing there is no reason for the scheduler to be "nice."

In the late 1990s I was able to achieve 10 times the throughput on an Oracle database server by tricking out the operating system to ignore "fairness."

I used the real time scheduler in HP-UX to permit Oracle to preempt everything else.

Color me skeptical, for two main reasons:

1. These AI-generated math proofs are very difficult for humans to read and comprehend, so we have to rely on automated proof-checkers such as Lean. AI is used to translate written math into computer code that Lean can check. We've already seen examples of mistranslation, the consequence of which is that the Lean-verified statement isn't equivalent to the statement written in ordinary math notation. We have also seen examples where a bug in Lean was exploited by the AI (which is basically brute-forcing its way to something Lean says is correct) to "verify" an incorrect proof. It takes time for humans to discover these, so all claims of AI proving something new are tentative.

2) The AI companies have an extremely strong incentive to sell the public on "recursive self-improvement" - it's their only ticket out of what otherwise looks like an economic bubble. RSI is basically a magic wand that turns implausible claims plausible, because it allows proponents to invoke unforseen technology created by a mysterious higher intelligence. Without RSI, these companies appear to be selling products for which there is nowhere near enough consumer demand to recoup their extravagent investments... which means the bubble has to pop. 

It's IPO season for AI companies, and selling the public on RSI is how they hope to overcome what looks like an increasingly nervous market. A huge dose of skepticism is called for here.

I asked if it was ok first. He was very accepting and had formed a special connection with our dog during the first hip replacement surgery over two years ago so he is special to us and our dog. That was the nicest hug I’ve had in a very long time. Most hugs don’t feel good. I know I have childhood issues with personal touch and I don’t need to work through that. I can just choose not to hug and ask before I expressing gratefulness first. My political activism began in 1956 when, at age ten, I proudly wore an "I LIKE IKE" campaign button to school. A bit later, childishly extolling the patriotism of "Tailgunner" Joe McCarthy, I won an American Legion speech contest. What was I thinking?

Then,  just as I was old enough to start actually thinking, along came Kennedy. I threw in my lot with his "Ask what you can do..." people and haven't looked back. 

JFK's murder, and Johnson's ascension to the Presidency in that cramped airplane in Dallas, rocked my altruistic young world. Who was this lumbering, boorish man, I thought, shoving the gauzy Camelot world aside and grabbing the reins of power with such eager hands?

I found out from his dizzying blizzard of Great Society accomplishments. This was a politician in the truest sense: arm-twisting, cajoling, wrangling, compromising, threatening, promising. Accruing and using power in the service of a bold vision for the good of our country.

Then came Vietnam, the Sword of Damocles that hung over Johnson--and the nation. The ferment and turmoil of the late sixties. His startling announcement on TV. And Johnson disappeared to his beloved hill country.

Lyndon Johnson, in my eyes was both hero and villain. I'm old now, old enough to see the naivete of the black-and-white certainty of my youth. I've seen and lived and learned enough to know that heroes have clay feet and, yes, some apparent villains accomplish great things.

When my husband was transferred to Houston from Manhattan in 1999, I thought there was nothing in Texas, but the concrete of the cities and the flat dusty roads between them. Then we decided to tour the hill country, starting at the  Austin Johnson library, then moving to the ladybird wildflower Center,, and then the ranch in Stonewall, the Johnson City Homestead of LBJ’s childhood   I remember parking on the road in front of the ranch and looking down to the Pedernales River and thinking, “this is what heaven must look like.” 

At that time, there was a jitney that took us from the LBJ visitor’s center to the important sites, including LBJ’s gravesite in the family cemetery. After the little bus was nearly filled, two black gentlemen came in and seated an older woman in the front, sitting down near her. When we reached the gravesite, the two gentlemen asked us if we would kindly wait a few minutes before they think the bus. Not a word was said, but the lady, Lady Bird herself, turned and smiled a thank you. Though she could not hear us as she knelt for a few  minutes at her husband‘s grave, the entire bus was  silent.  A black limousine took her away. That encounter inspired my sons’ interest in history and politics. It was a lovely moment that allowed us to see our new state in a different light. 

LBJ said that the Civil Rights Act would cost the Democrats the South for a generation.  I hope that somewhere he knows that we got it back for him.

The challenge is to establish a common identify for political stability and unity in national emergences to enable common efforts to resolve common challenges. 

When racial, life style, and gender segregated people before the mid-1960's, this unifying identity was described as the melting pot and it was heralded by the phrase, E pluribus unum.  But the melting pot notion fell out of favor because it was believed to demand that people reject the cultures of their ancestors in favor of an insipid and shallow common identity, one which condoned racial discrimination and injustices against marginalized minorities. The multicultural ideal replaced it, but multiculturalism results in pluralism that amounts to insular groups that only interact in a few situations, mostly in employment and in public schools. Communities are established which are de facto segregation. 

Diversity is not immoral or any threat to individual liberties but it tends to try to resolve group correlated inequities by making distributions accord with desired proportionalities rather than attempting to rectify the causes of inequities. Underserved communities and under funded public schools result in undereducated graduates with far fewer opportunities to improve their circumstances. Trying to achieve proportional distributions to eliminate disproportionate distributions after people have reached maturity unprepared to thrive has been the public policy. Children must have the same opportunities.

Fascist Germany that waged war for dominance over Europe, is now NATO and EU trusted ally. Yet, the Soviet Union (now Russia), pivotal in defeating fascist Germany, is now treated as Europe's arch enemy. Do we value fascism more than forging relations with Russia? Let's look at Iran. In 1953, to gain control over Iran's vast oil resources, the USA and Britain (Project BOOT/AJAX), mastermind the overthrow of Iran's democratically elected government. Reinstalling dictator Shah Pahlavi created the pathway to Iran's theocracy. Thus, the current war on Iran finds its roots in 1953's disastrous Project BOOT/AJAX. Why have we not learned that hegemony, i.e., seeking control through isolation, sanctions, and war, is not effective long-term foreign policy? Why not try diplomatic relations with Russia and Iran instead? We see the current outcome of bad policy in the current midterm elections. comments.name: Tim B
comments.body:
Donald Trump did not inherit an inevitable war with Iran. He helped dismantle the diplomatic framework designed to prevent one.

In 2015, the Obama administration and five other world powers negotiated a nuclear agreement that restricted Iran's uranium enrichment, reduced its nuclear stockpile and imposed extensive international inspections. The International Atomic Energy Agency verified Iran's compliance with its central nuclear commitments.

Then, in May 2018, Trump unilaterally abandoned the agreement, despite that record of compliance. His promised better deal never materialized...surprised?

What followed? Iran progressively violated enrichment limits, expanded its nuclear activities, and restricted international monitoring. The very dangers the agreement had successfully constrained became substantially worse.

On February 28, 2026, Trump joined Israel in launching military strikes against Iran, igniting a devastating regional war.

The staggering irony is that Trump destroyed an agreement limiting Iran's nuclear ambitions, then launched a war partly justified by the nuclear danger that grew after his withdrawal.

That is not brilliant diplomacy. That is a catastrophic failure of judgment, followed by military force to confront a crisis his own decisions helped intensify.

America deserves leadership, not reckless decisions followed by expensive attempts to repair the damage.

This is a bit of a stretch. We talk about "seismic changes," "tornadoes," "hurricanes," "floods," etc., all the time to metaphorically describe societal and political phenomena. That doesn't mean we are less sympathetic to people who have suffered from actual natural disasters. 

As for Hokusai's "Great Wave," it has been called "the most reproduced artwork in history." I doubt if anyone is really surprised that it showed up on the front page of the New York Post. In Japan you can buy all manner of tchotchkes, from keychains to boxer shorts, embellished with the "Great Wave." In fact, there's a good chance you would buy them with a ¥1000 bill, every one of which has, wait for it, Hokusai's "Great Wave" engraved on it. This work of art could not be more monetized!

I have lived in Japan since the 1970s. Nice try in finding an angle for your story, but for my Japanese friends and acquaintances, this is simply not an issue.

comments.name: Tall Trees and Trains

I’ve seen much more subversive use of Japanese imagery about Japanese and world politics in a two story exhibition in a sky scraper next to a train station in Tokyo. 

 The quote “Hokusai depicted a powerful, dynamic wave, so to see that transformed into a parody — a kind of ironic subversion — is something we cannot view favorably [publicly in front of others. Particularly if they are foreign reporters],” 
<
That quote, is the most Japanese thing ever. Yes the part I added is the part left on said. And in Japanese, context is key. And what is left unsaid is often implied by context and left unexplained. For example, plural does not exist. Like with  deer, moose, or fish it is understood by context. 

I mean if lady asks is she looks fat, the correct answer is rarely “yes”. Same deal. 

You expect a museum official to say it’s okay to anyone; let alone an American reporter?

comments.name: Mochi Mochi
comments.body:
Hokusai died in poverty in 1849. Neither he nor his family made any money from his famous woodblock print The Great Wave.  Thousands of prints were made, reportedly selling as cheaply as a bowl of noodles. Hokusai was paid for his design, but never got any royalties or money from the sales. An original of this print recently fetched $2.8 million at Sotheby’s. 

The Great Wave is in the public domain now, and as we have seen, it can be copied freely.  It’s all around us.  Last year I visited the Hokusai Museum in Obuse, Japan, which had an amusing exhibition showing the myriad of objects that have embraced the popularity of this print.  When I entered the lobby, I was greeted by a large soda machine with The Great Wave painted on it. 

I come from a family of Japanese woodblock printers, and Hokusai’s story makes me very sad. Others may feel differently, but to me, the prevalence of this print has cheapened its beauty.

Japanese institutions should be equally mindful of the severe historical trauma the Rising Sun flag evokes across East Asia due to its association with imperial aggression. True cultural respect isn't a one-sided expectation. It is about recognizing that whether dealing with artistic heritage or historical military symbols, we all benefit when we listen to what causes pain to others.

These latest book contestants fit the formula of no plot except for maybe one of the gay identity books and the alien takeover of Britain— but I get the sense that even they lack any type of real developed plot, and deal more with the psychological and loneliness issues of nonconformity (I.e. this character is special— whatever).

One has the backdrop of the 2024 election along with some whiny windbag’s loneliness and suicidal tendencies. What a bore.

To the commenter who said “I struggle to understand what’s politically correct” she must not have read any of these books or even the synopses. 

What a condescending comment on her part — Charlene was absolutely correct.

Every Booker Prize winner or National Book Award winner is plotless, lacks character development and engaging characters and is a real bore to read— they all have been the same for so many years— I can name many books with more humor than “Black Bag.”

Cause and effect in a two-sentence paragraph:
"The SAT tests went online in 2024, a move aimed partly at ending test leaks. But, looking to capitalize on consumer demand for high scores, scammers have devised a medley of tricks to undermine the security of the digital test."

If you want students to be just themselves when taking the tests, then you need to airgap the tests.  Really, in the connected world we've created, you have to put intrusive effort into making sure the tests are taken offline, and the students can't leave with copies of anything they can't memorize.

I can understand not wanting to go back to paper, but an alternative that uses digital tests would be to make sure of a few things:
- test is on a device with NO NETWORK ACCESS
- students are not allowed to bring ANY recording devices in - and really, ANY.  No phones, no cameras, none of the creepy recording glasses Zuckerberg is pushing.
- lockers for student's stuff, OUTSIDE the testing room
- have paper notebooks and pens available for scratch work and collect those, or have tablets that can be used for scratch work but they also have no network access and remain in the room.

Or perhaps an easier alternative, since the urge to cheat is so considerable - flood the market with many different sets of tests containing combinations of correct and incorrect answers. Fight availability of tests by drowning the copies out with ones that will cause failure.

I am a Toyota fan.

Own a RAV4 Prime Plug-in hybrid.

Toyota’s hybrids have two especially interesting technologies most people—even owners—aren’t aware of:

1) the transmissions use a central sun gear surrounded by four planetary gears and the design is simply bulletproof. Properly maintain them according to specs and they will never be the reason you sell the car.

2) the gas engine is not like other gas engines. Most are what’s called Otto cycle, which are great off the line but not great for efficiency. Toyota’s gas engines are not Otto cycle, they are Atkinson cycle— terrible off the line but amazing efficiency at highway speeds.

But the thing is you don’t need off-the-line acceleration if you have an electric motor to take that piece. Electric motors are amazing off the line!

So you get the best of both.

And that’s why Toyota and not another maker’s hybrid for me.

My husband and I studied adolescence and youth for decades--from a developmental and cohort-generational perspective--at first in the U.S., then historically and globally. I will spare you some fascinating details, but here are some takeaways:

1. Adolescence is a time of leaving childhood and striving for independence (a healthy thing, but not easily navigated). Combative, not listening, determined, experimenting for themselves, and trying to figure it out. Adult neglect and abandonment as well as hovering and smothering can be detrimental--but so can not having challenges, difficulties, criticisms, weaknesses, and failures to overcome to prepare young people to deal with adulthood. 

2. Also, a common theme from troubled teens and college students turns out to be when parents missed the moments and did not enjoy their growing children and teens. Too strict and dour, or too preoccupied to appreciate and enjoy their teens (parents, teachers, coaches, bosses, and entire societies). 

We asked the question how similar or different are teens and youth around the world. Piecing together youth research over time and across countries, bottom line: young people are quite similar in the goals for life, appreciation for their families and education, oriented toward optimism, and a desire to be heard and contribute. How easy or difficult do societies make that for them? In general, but at the individual level and anecdotally, some youth really struggle and need affirmation & support.

Improving mental health statistics probably indicate kids and parents are adapting to what we now know is dangerous about social media, smartphones, etc. We’re learning to treat dangerous technology as something dangerous. That wouldn’t have been true for kids who came of age in the 2010-2020 period.

That shows that research and public awareness are both helpful in mitigating the harm these technologies can cause. However, it’s still a half-solution. We are leaving children and families mostly on their own to manage the risks. The kids who are in grade school today are the teenagers whose mental health will reflect the change.

The world needs denuclearization, but it is absurd to expect China to jeopardize its security by either cutting its arsenal or agreeing to not increase it.  Too bad, but that's realpolitik—which Xi understands thoroughly and Trump not at all.

The writer does not mention the 1919 Treaty of Versailles.  It turned over prominent Chinese territory previously occupied by Germany to Japan instead of returning it to China, one of the allies, and it led to China being the only major power not to sign.   To this day, the humiliation is remembered, and China commemorates its response annually as Wusi Yundong, the May Fourth Movement. It is known to all.  

This historical detail matters because mistreatment by foreign powers is a steadfast theme in China's history, and a firm basis for Mr. Xi's ongoing wariness.

China already regards itself as superior to the US, and its economy by PPP is far larger. Xi sees no need to boost China's prestige. It exists as a fact.

We are living through a sea change in how consumers purchase and receive goods, and our policies have not kept pace. We need protections for both consumers and delivery workers established at the municipal, state, or federal level. Otherwise, companies trying to do the right thing will be pushed out by competitors offering cheaper delivery. Competition with Amazon has only intensified the pressure to keep delivery costs as low as possible.
Here in San Francisco delivery workers are under enormous pressure to meet daily quotas--packages are left on doorsteps (and stolen) or delivered to the wrong addresses. Amazon is hardly alone in using third-party delivery services. FedEx Ground operates under a similar contracting model, and even USPS contracts out certain delivery routes.

Then there is the army of DoorDash and Instacart workers moving through San Francisco. California's Proposition 22 provides some protections for app-based drivers, but it also preserves their independent-contractor status. Between these gig workers and drivers employed by third-party delivery contractors, I feel as though we have created practically a modern slave class.
I would certainly pay a little more for delivery if it meant meaningful worker protections and greater accountability to consumers. But individual goodwill will not solve a systemic problem. Without enforceable standards that apply across the industry, companies that pay and treat workers better risk being undercut by those that do not.

comments.body: I served on a jury may years ago, and it was fascinating. One thing I learnt was, that if a defendant calls in character references (apart from their partner), then the prosecution can call in their previous history. Brand had no character references, ergo he very likely had something in the cupboard.

comments.name: Jon
comments.body:
The use of past convictions is debatable; while it would provide some context to the alleged crime, on balance, it is, in my view, not actual evidence of the crime being judged in any given trial.
It is possible (and I am not a lawyer) that if the defendant is found guilty, those past offences will be taken into consideration during sentencing.

The only evidence presented at trial, therefore, is that of what the defendant is accused of. I wonder what our American cousins think of that.

On another note, I am surprised that American journalists are bound by such rules when reporting this in the US. Because of your First Amendment, is the compliance from American journalists purely voluntary?

comments.name: thefullview
comments.body:
The U.S. media has made court coverage a branch of show business -- cheap, highly profitable entertainment. Trial by perverse media circus in some cases. 

British law, though it may be imperfect, gets it more right. A court of law should have firm boundaries when it comes to the privacy of all involved: lawyers, judges, defendants and witnesses.

What I find just as disturbing is how body cameras on U.S. cops, which was a well-intentioned attempt to instill more public trust in law enforcement, has become a prurient cottage industry on social media, punishing private citizens far beyond what most court cases would or could bring. Publicly accessible footage of citizens interacting with police -- often in moments of personal crisis -- becomes the modern equivalent of putting them in medieval stocks for public abuse, with literally no trial. 

I wonder if British law is better than we are on that front as well.

I just finished reading a book about the 1953 CIA coup that overthrew the democratically elected government of Mohammad Mossadegh in Iran. That coup,  closely followed by another in Guatemala that overthrew the democratically elected government of Jacobo Arbenz, empowered the CIA and also the Dulles brothers, fanatical cold warriors who exercised enormous power in the Eisenhower administration. 

Those coups established covert action as perhaps the preeminent role of the CIA, and throughout the following decades, the agency engineered a long list of coups and assassinations, most often against democratically elected leaders deemed insufficiently supportive of US geopolitical and corporate interests. It almost certainly had a hand in the murder of Patrice Lumumba just months before the crash that killed Hammarskjold. Anyone who believes that accusations of American involvement in the crash are mere conspiracy theories should read about the history of the CIA's dirty tricks.  I only hope that the UN's investigation succeeds in overcoming US stonewalling and sheds light on what really happened.

comments.name: Cate
comments.body:
It would be so incredibly satisfying--even sensational--if, just for once, we as a viewing public just got up and left the theater as a gesture that expressed our deeply questioned or even outraged response to our, yet again, being subjected to the content of a film described as a "laugh-and-blood-flecked romp".

To begin with: isn't "laughter and blood-flecked" rather an oxymoron?

The constancy of the notion that we, as viewers, must be perpetually forced to accept as "entertainment" all of the violence, all of the meaningless gestures of supposed power and control over others as even capable of being humorous; our lack of expectations, instead, of our being outraged, upset, our feeling abused even.

No: there we are thinking that we're being "entertained", quietly and passively--always expected to consider violence-filled visual fare as absolutely worthy of our time or attention without question.

Does this type of filmmaking even qualify as "entertainment"--and, if so, how so?

It is time for a serious search of ourselves to find out about our values; what are our preferences when it comes to what we view, and get a clear grasp about what we believe to constitute what we consider to be our pleasures, our beliefs, our inner dialogue.

This type of filmmaking isn't art, not even entertainment, really: it's just mindless perpetuation of the violent decline of our values.

I say boycott violence in pictures and streamed content--let's take back the dignity of our lives

The new budget has laudable goals, but the question I would watch over the next 5 years is whether the investments are generating enough economic growth to keep debt-to-GDP from rising materially above 40%? That's the sustainability test.

Further, there are implications that are not going to make many environmentalist happy. To pay for that budget, Canada is going to have to sell a lot of oil. But the key to the Carney government’s ultimate success will be whether they can foster an increase in productivity.

If productivity does not rise, budgets just like this one will prove to be a disaster in the long run. The average American reader needs to understand that Canadian productivity has been cratering for years, and Canada‘s only path forward is to outgrow the deficit.

But my real concern is with defense. They have spent billions on capital acquisitions such as the submarines and so forth, but the Department of National Defence is in fact operating under an austerity budget that is forcing painful choices and trade-offs.

But for a Liberal government, this budget is a welcome departure from a decade of fiscal mismanagement under that moron Trudeau. Carney, in that sense is a welcome saviour.

Slow and steady it should be, always remembering that there is no 'normal' to which we can return, while enjoying the steady improvements that have and will come from diversification in international trade.

Further, Canadians have been victimized by the USA enough times that almost nobody wants to become MORE dependent upon the USA than we currently are.

It’s apocryphal now, but the response from (possibly) either Zhou En Lai or Chairman Mao, following the same question asked of Kissinger years ago about how they perceived the outcome of the French Revolution, and following a 30 minute responses / lecture from Kissinger was, more accurately, "I think it’s too soon to tell.’ 

That’s pretty much where Canadians are now. Give the USA another 15 or 20 years to see how the dust settles, then move cautiously.

This guy seems to have been competent in many walks of life.  He certainly could have learned the fundamentals of sailing.  I can infer that the boat was around 50+ years old because it has a wood mast on a pulpit.  They simply don’t make them like that, anymore.  The boat is pretty.  In its day the voyage would not have been foolhardy.  The boat was not the problem.

The issue that has me shaking my head is that he either did know how to reef(lessen) the sail area or wasn’t sufficiently drilled.  If you don’t have modern equipment for shortening sails, you better be able to reef, literally, in your sleep & in the dark.  Boats of that era equipped for voyages, would have also carried  storm sails.  Storm sails can substitute in an emergency, but he had no hope of retreating to the west coast against the prevailing winds or going forward to Hawaii.

There are so many good books, that is impossible that he could not have acquired the practical knowledge he needed  He didn’t appear to have analog self-steering gear.  He didn’t know to put a little bleach in the water.  It isn’t a great taste, but it will preserve the water.

Personally, I lost the ability to sail offshore between 75-77.  Everyone is different, but I have 55+ years of experience in craft of his boat’s age through to the most modern aluminum hulled craft with every modern aid one can imagine.

I think the boat could have done the trip.  Obviously, the skipper could not.

I was a maritime cargo attorney for 38 years (1979-2017). Our Constitution also gives concurrent state jurisdiction--but how do you toll a statute of limitations when you have to serve a defunct defendant. The answer is filing an action in a Federal district court with the closest venue to the incident. In this case it was Norfolk.

You can then try to serve the defendant(s), or, if (like the majority of my cases) the parties were already negotiating, it buys time and provides a process for resolution of the litigated claims.

comments.body:
New Zealand has a serious problem with its political conversation. Our television news can be relentlessly alarmist, often more interested in outrage and political point-scoring than giving people a balanced understanding of what's actually happening.

We're a small country with small-country problems, yet somehow our politicians manage to make everything feel like a national crisis.

I'm actually quite happy to see young New Zealanders heading overseas. Get out. See the world. Experience different cultures, economies and ways of thinking. Some will come home, as I did, with a much greater appreciation of just how lucky we were to grow up here. Perspective is a useful thing.

What New Zealand desperately needs is someone like James Talarico in its political conversation. Someone who can articulate an argument, think independently, speak intelligently and, above all, tell the truth without constantly resorting to political theatre.

Our politicians seem so preoccupied with pushing each other out of the picture that they've forgotten the most important part of the job: giving people something worth listening to.

I'm less interested in another round of political mudslinging than I am in hearing someone explain where we're going, why we're going there, and how we're going to make this country better.

Surely that's not too much to ask.

Meloni’s plan with Albania for Italy is more legally defensible under European human rights law: properly trained and experienced Italian immigration officials located in Albania decide the asylum claims of immigrants entering Italy and sent to Albania for “processing”; there is a right of appeal against any adverse decision to the Italian courts; and successful claimants are given asylum in Italy not Albania. Though Meloni’s scheme is legally far more defensible than the ham fisted  British effort, the Italian approach is a much weaker weapon against illegal entry by bogus asylum seekers.

comments.name: Erik Frederiksen

Climate change accelerates the risk of future pandemics by altering ecosystems and driving ecological disruption on a global scale. 

As global temperatures rise and habitats shift, wildlife species—particularly bats, rodents, and insects—are forced to migrate toward cooler regions and higher elevations, bringing disparate species into contact for the first time. 

These novel interactions create ideal conditions for viral spillover and the emergence of new zoonotic pathogens. 

Concurrently, expanding vector ranges bring diseases like dengue and malaria to previously temperate regions, while extreme weather events displace human populations, damaging sanitation infrastructure and weakening healthcare access.

To mitigate these intensifying threats, proactive pandemic preparedness and early planning are essential. 

Traditional reactive approaches, which rely on responding after an outbreak begins, are insufficient against rapidly evolving global health risks. 

Robust planning requires establishing comprehensive surveillance systems to monitor wildlife-human interfaces, investing in resilient public health infrastructure, and strengthening international data sharing. 

Integrating environmental and climate forecasting into public health frameworks allows governments to anticipate spillover hotspots and allocate resources before localized outbreaks transform into global catastrophes.

This expensive winter hobby or lifestyle contributes to environmental pollution and ecological damage primarily through travel carbon emissions and intensive resort operations. It also damages and disturbs wildlife habitats and natural environments. If this winter’s anticipated natural windfalls are expected to draw more visitors and increase activities at ski resorts, implementing added costs might be an appropriate way to deter or mitigate excessive pollution and environmental damage.

The federal government should consider levying excise taxes or assessing environmental protection fees on ski-related activities at popular destinations during peak seasons. The collected tax and fee revenues could be used to aid other regions negatively affected by these unusual weather patterns as well as to restore environmental damage in those ski areas.

While people have the freedom to choose their lifestyles, they also need to be responsible and make an effort to help remedy environmental damages they cause.

I have LONG said AC is a very well kept secret.

These days we own in Margate. When prices started climbing we considered other beach towns like LBI. Because of AC, I simply could not. In the years since the shopping, imax, Boardwalk memories, we found so many other ways of loving AC. We have gone to some really fun concerts—Steely Dan, Idina Menzell, Train among others. We have grown to LOVE the secret restaurants that only in the knows can frequent like Chef Volas, Angelos or Knife and Fork. We love the fact that our adult children can easily take buses down to the casinos from NYC and get to us with minimal hassle. I love the redevelopment including Stockston State.

But the thing i love the most about AC?

THE HISTORY. I love that city so much. I hope it gets the love it deserves. The citizens of AC deserve better services and support and opportunities. Crime is still unacceptably high.

But when you study the birth of resort towns, AC is right front and center. It’s a national treasure worth preserving.

Atlantic City is exceptionally vulnerable to sea level rise due to low barrier island elevation, severe coastal land subsidence, and high asset density. Local relative sea level along the New Jersey coast has risen over 18 inches since 1911—more than double the global average. This rate is driven by thermal expansion, melting ice, and regional land settling.

Because much of the city sits just feet above high tide, sunny-day flooding already occurs routinely. Back-bay areas face the highest risk: rising tides block gravity-fed drainage outlets, trapping rainwater and flooding streets from within. 

Climate models project local sea levels will rise an additional 1.4 to 2.1 feet by 2050, making high-tide flooding a frequent occurrence and exposing critical infrastructure to severe storm surges. In response, the city is investing tens of millions into high-capacity back-bay stormwater pump stations, elevated bulkheads, and utility retrofits to maintain resilience.

Here is the opposite viewpoint from ChatGPT:

The New York Times suggests that when someone from our past contacts us, we should examine our feelings, question their motives, and carefully assess whether reconnecting would be emotionally beneficial.

But an important body of psychological research suggests almost the opposite.

Psychologists Lara Aknin and Gillian Sandstrom have demonstrated that people are surprisingly reluctant to reconnect with old friends, even when they genuinely want to do so. Peggy Liu and her colleagues found that people underestimate how much an unexpected message is appreciated. And Nicholas Epley's research demonstrates that we routinely anticipate more awkwardness and less enjoyment from social encounters than we actually experience.

In other words, the very psychological calculations that are supposed to protect us may be preventing us from enjoying rewarding human relationships.

Perhaps we should stop treating every invitation from the past as a potential emotional threat.

Instead of asking six complicated questions before answering an old friend's message, why not ask just one: **What wonderful experience might I miss if I say no?**

Sometimes the psychologically healthier choice may be to stop analyzing and start living.

**Less hesitation. More curiosity. More human connection.**

———
A Sonnet, Slightly Out of Tune

A fourteen-line design of metered verse,
Where iambs march in steady, patterned stride,
To frame a thought, a blessing, or a curse,
With secrets that the final lines decide.

It opens with a formal, strict constraint,
Where rhyming pairs construct a clever cage,
To sing a lover’s heavy, sweet complaint,
Or capture fleeting beauty on the page.

But look! The rigid rules must now give way,
A dis-so-nant dis-cord may split the chord,
To show how human passions truly play,
Before the final harmony's restored.

For flawless songs are cold and empty things;
It is the cracked and wounded heart that sings.

comments.body: I'm not trying to shift the subject, but when reading the one kid talking about parent's overzealous protection causing children to adopt a nervous and fearful lens through which they view the world, I couldn't help but notice what feels like a parallel/interconnected phenomenon. I have met many, many people, and have several friends who carry firearms for protection. Some when they're going into a city or new place, some when they're going fishing, hiking, or into the "wilderness", and some on a daily basis. None of these people are criminals or live a lifestyle that would have them more exposed to violence or require them to defend themselves. It's all a big what if, like the what if a kidnapper snatches my 8 year old off the street because I wasn't watching. What most of these folks would call being prepared and ready to defend themselves and others seems like, at least in the cases of those I know, to be purely a fear based conditioning that was likely passed down by their parents, peers, media, etc. I'm not saying this applies to everyone who carries a firearm, there are many areas, lifestyles and personal histories that make personal protection a good idea. My point is how many people carry them around needlessly because they were brought up to view others with suspicion and fear, particularly if they don't fit their "in" group.
